job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a room with my mate Liam in a rented terrace in Sunderland, so I'm usually up early to give him the desk. I go through the job boards, send a few applications, then take a bus to my dad's garage where I help out for cash a couple of days a week, mostly sweeping and fetching parts. In the evening it's five-a-side with the lads, and then more applications. I try to be doing something every hour, because sitting still makes me think.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, and I passed with an average result. My final project was a stock system for a local hardware shop, so the owner could see what was running low. It worked, and he still uses it, but he never offered me a job, which stung. I didn't get an internship because they all asked for a placement year, and I'd had to work to pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's see some proof. At the garage the lads would say it's all talk, and they'd be right most of the time. I'd tell my mates that people who work hard will be fine regardless. Online I'd stay out of it, because nobody needs my opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes nothing for me, which means I'm still stuck. The jobs for junior developers round here are mainly in Newcastle, and each one has two hundred applicants. I use an AI tool now and then for my CV, but it hasn't made any difference to getting an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending applications, thirty or so a month, and look at Newcastle and Leeds. I'd keep helping at my dad's garage and ask whether the owner would let me do their booking system for a fee. I'd also try to get a bit of IT support work, something like fixing office computers, because you've got to start somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired. It's not scary, it's more a grind. I've been doing this for months, and my dad says it's not about doing the right thing, it's about the right person seeing you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad said it's about the right person seeing you. Do you agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. Half the jobs go to someone's cousin. I don't resent that, it's how people work. But I haven't got a cousin in tech, so I need to get in front of people, at meetups and trade shows, and that costs bus fares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad pays me about eighty a week, and I put in fifty towards the rent. I've no savings, and the student loan will start taking money once I'm earning. I'm not asking for handouts, but I'd take a decent job tomorrow.

Online I'd stay out of it, because nobody needs my opinion.
think: Nothing changes for me, so I'm still stuck: **two hundred applicants** per junior job.
AI hasn't helped me get a single interview.

Offer to build the garage's **booking system** for a fee.
Try for IT support work fixing office computers.
feel: Tired: it's a **grind**, not a scare.
Told by my dad that it's about the right person seeing me.

Offer to build the garage a paid booking system
Apply for IT support jobs fixing office computers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, work changes, always has. At the garage I'd say it's a bit like when computers came into the workshop, some people hated it and then couldn't live without it. Online I'd say keep the training local, and don't pay people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd say coding and testing are exactly what gets taken first, so I'm in the wrong line of work at the wrong time. My real edge might be that I'm practical, I like fixing things, and I've worked in a garage. That's something a screen can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools properly, not just for my CV, and I'd look for jobs where software meets real things, like IT support, telecoms or factory systems. I'd do a short course in networking or cybersecurity, because firms always need that kind of person. I'd ask my dad's customers if anyone needed someone to look after their systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit rattled, but less than I'd have thought. I'm not the type to sit around. I'd rather throw myself at it and find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who thinks it's all over for software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software isn't over, but the easy start is. The ones who can do both, the software and the real-world bit, will still have jobs. Learn how a business actually works, and be useful on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't pay people to sit at home. What do you mean exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think support should come with something to do, like training or work. Nobody should go hungry, but I don't want a country where a whole generation is told to wait. When I was a kid my dad took night classes, and I think that's the model.

Online I'd say keep training local and tie support to work.

steps.text: Use an AI tool daily for coding practice and applications
Take an evening networking or cybersecurity course
Apply for IT support and telecoms jobs near Sunderland

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too quick, and the government and the big firms have a duty to people. At the garage the lads would say what about the robots, and I'd say they're three years behind, so we've got a little time. Online I'd keep it short: get ready, look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's about as bad as it can be. Computing work is gone in two years, and I'm only at the start of it. At the same time, I'd have three years of hands-on work before the robots, if I'm quick. My dad's garage is safe until about 2031, then who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into hands-on work straight away: garage, mechanics, electrical or factory jobs, anything with tools. I'd ask my dad to train me properly on cars, especially the electric ones. I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food, and start a savings jar with whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest, though I'd not show it at the garage. It's the kind of fear where you've got a lot of energy and nowhere to put it. I'd be running before I knew where to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, teach me what you know, from the engine to the invoices. He'd say he's been waiting for that for years. We'd probably have an argument about it first, and then the best weekend of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about Liam, who shares your room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight that we should both cut costs and maybe look for a cheaper place. He works in a call centre, so he's in the first group to go. I'd help him find hands-on work too, because mates don't leave mates.

say: I'd say it's **too quick**, and big firms and government have a duty to people.
Online I'd keep it short: get ready and look after each other.

My dad's garage is safe until about 2031.

steps.text: Ask my dad to train me on engines and electric cars
Apply for mechanic, electrical and factory jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's time to get ready, and we should make the most of it. I'd tell my mates to learn something practical and keep it up. Online I'd say apprenticeships and local training are better than waiting on government schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is enough to put a plan in place. I could get a first job in IT in the next year or so, learn what the company does, and move across into the technical side. By 2031 I'd have a few years behind me and some cash, which is a decent position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first IT or support job and work like mad. I'd keep helping at my dad's garage on Saturdays, learning the trade. I'd put a quarter of my pay into savings and sign up for a short electrical or networking course on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit hopeful. I'd have something to aim at. It's the first one where I can see myself working somewhere in 2031 and doing fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't panic-buy tools and I wouldn't drop my software skills. I'd do both together for a few years, then choose. With two years I'd have to jump at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about moving away for the first job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it for a good one. I'd rather stay near my family, but a year in Leeds or Manchester is fine. I'd share a room again, and I'd come home on weekends when I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no need to make a fuss. I'd tell people to keep doing honest work and keep learning. Online I'd say that I think the schools should be teaching hands-on skills along with the screen stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I can have a proper career and still be ready for 2036. I'd be thirty-three. I'd have a job, a mortgage, maybe a family, and a skill that robots take a while to match. I think I'd be alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with an IT job, put in three or four good years, and learn how the firm runs. I'd study at night for a recognised qualification, maybe in networks or electrical systems. I'd start saving for a deposit as soon as I'm earning, and I'd probably help my dad with the garage on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. I'd feel it's like a long season. You can plan, you can train, and you can take your time over it, as long as you don't switch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about a family in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like a partner and kids by thirty or so. I'd want to be in a steady job when that happened, not scrambling. I'd put that in my plan, so it's not left to luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get too comfortable and miss the signs. Or my first job takes a long time to come, and the ten years shrink to seven. So I'd keep checking each year that I'm further on than the year before.

I'd say schools should teach hands-on skills alongside screen skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be at the start of my career with nothing behind me, and my trade would be the next to go. What would help is a decent chance to learn on the job, apprenticeships that take graduates, and honest talk from the people at the top about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that most lads I know would take any decent job and work hard at it. We're not asking for much. Give us a start and a bit of patience, and we'll do the rest.

headlineQuote: Most lads I know would take any decent job and work hard at it.
portrait: **David**, 23, passed computer science and shares a rented room with his mate Liam in Sunderland.
He helps at his father's garage for about **eighty pounds** a week and plays five-a-side most evenings.
Traditional and steady, he wants **work, not handouts**, and uses AI tools now and then, more when needed.
He thinks about practical routes where software meets real things, and plans with sports-season patience.
His mood is anxious in most worlds, alarmed when the warning is two years, and uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries him most: he'd have nothing behind him and his trade would be next.
He worries for his flatmate Liam too.
whatWouldHelp: A decent chance to **learn on the job**, with apprenticeships that take graduates.
Honest talk from the people at the top about what's coming.
